text: At closing time, the city lowers its eyelids, and the vault begins to breathe.
Behind the counter, a clock gives the crew exactly ninety seconds.
No faces are needed; only gloves, metal, and the patience of machines.
The vault door turns, slow as a planet, then gives way.
Inside, money sits in obedient stacks, waiting to become weather.
The alarm does not scream; it blooms, red and silent, across glass.
A camera watches the first runner cross marble towards the night.
Outside, rain needles the windscreen of a waiting black car.
The driver touches the wheel, and the street folds open.
Tyres bite water; headlights split traffic into silver animals.
Behind them, police lights gather, blue and red, like weather forming.
Above the avenue, a helicopter holds the chase in its cold eye.
They take the tunnel because tunnels forgive speed and hide direction.
For twenty seconds, the city becomes concrete, echo, and white lines.
At the bridge, the river appears underneath, black and suddenly wide.
One police car slides sideways, harmlessly, scattering rain across headlights.
The briefcase on the back seat remains perfectly still.
That is the oddity: panic everywhere, and the case behaves like ballast.
A phone screen lights once, showing a simple message: now.
The getaway car does not turn towards the motorway; it descends.
Down in the car park, engines fade, footsteps continue, measured and dry.
They leave the money beside a pillar, as if returning lost property.
By dawn, police surround an empty road, counting what was never stolen.
The vault is open, the notes remain, and the records are gone.
Ninety seconds was not the robbery. It was the distraction.
Somewhere beyond the city, a train carries silence into the morning.
